source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching (ICML)
finding: Needle-in-haystack where question and needle share almost no words, so the model must infer a latent link. Models that are near perfect at short length collapse at 32K. This is the machine version of the claim that a literal match is a crutch, not the whole of memory.
numbers: 13 LLMs that claim 128K+ context. 11 of 13 fall to half or less of their short-context base score at 32K. GPT-4o: 99.3% base to 69.7% at 32K. Llama 3.1 70B: 94.3% base to 42.7% at 32K, effective length only 2K (vs 32K on RULER).
quote: Even models enhanced with reasoning capabilities or CoT prompting struggle to maintain performance in long contexts.
limits: Synthetic needles (character names, attributes); English; filtered with Llama 3.3 70B. Measures retrieval from context, not an external store.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on word overlap between query and stored note. When cue and memory share no words, retrieval from long context degrades fast. Write notes with the likely query vocabulary and distinctive handles.

source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching (ICML) [literal-match ablation]
finding: Adding a literal match back (answer options that name the needle's character) restores most of the lost accuracy. Direct questions that quote the needle word are easy at any length. So the match, not the memory, carries performance.
numbers: Llama 3.3 70B at 8K/16K/32K: direct (needle word in question) 98.3/98.5/98.5; one-hop no match 84.1/73.2/56.2; one-hop with literal match (multiple choice) 98.7/97.4/93.1; two-hop no match 57.4/42.7/25.9; two-hop with match 96.3/94.6/87.2.
limits: One model for this ablation. The multiple-choice format also shrinks the search space, so the gain mixes match and format. Table text was column-interleaved in the PDF; the row-to-hop assignment is the most likely reading.
agent_relevance: Supports the encoding-specificity reading (match helps) and the critique (match is a shortcut that hides weak association). Test the agent with and without overlap between query and note.

source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching (ICML) [distractors and CoT]
finding: Literal matches can also hurt: an irrelevant passage that shares words with the question lowers accuracy on the correct but lexically distant needle. Chain-of-thought helps only a little because the question cannot be decomposed.
numbers: With distractors present (GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B), normalized score falls below the 0.85 effective threshold at shorter length than without. Two-hop with CoT still poor at 16K and above. Exact per-length distractor numbers are in figures only.
limits: Figure-only numbers; two models.
agent_relevance: A lexically close wrong note beats a semantically right note. Rank by distinctiveness of the match, not by raw overlap. Extra reasoning steps do not repair a failed lookup.

source: Sciavolino, Zhong, Lee, Chen (2021) Simple Entity-Centric Questions Challenge Dense Retrievers (EMNLP)
finding: Dense (semantic) retrievers do worse than plain BM25 on simple questions about rare entities. The distinctive token (a rare name) is a better key than a learned similarity.
numbers: EntityQuestions top-20 accuracy: DPR trained on NQ 49.7% average vs BM25 72.0%; gap up to 60 points on some question types. DPR trained on 4 datasets 56.7% average. 'Where was [E] born?': BM25 beats DPR by 49.9 points. REALM 19.6% average, far below BM25. Capital-of question: DPR 80.1 vs BM25 64.4 (DPR wins on the common pattern).
limits: Pre-LLM dense retrievers (DPR, REALM); not generative LLMs. Wikipedia passages. Dense models do better on common entities.
agent_relevance: In agent memory, keep an exact-term (lexical or ID) route next to the semantic one. Distinctive names, ids and numbers are strong keys.

source: Sciavolino, Zhong, Lee, Chen (2021) Simple Entity-Centric Questions Challenge Dense Retrievers (EMNLP) [popularity bias and fixes]
finding: DPR accuracy falls as the entity gets rarer, while BM25 is much less sensitive to entity frequency. Fine-tuning on one question pattern fixes that pattern only. A better passage encoder closes most of the gap.
numbers: Entities grouped in 8 frequency buckets by Wikipedia link count. Fine-tuning only the passage encoder gave 72.8 / 84.2 / 78.0 on three templates vs BM25 75.3 / 85.0 / 72.6; question-encoder-only gave 45.4 / 72.8 / 73.4. Data augmentation did not fix generalisation.
limits: Three templates studied in depth (place of birth, headquarters, creator). Which template maps to which column read from layout text.
agent_relevance: Index-side (write-time) representation matters more than query-side tweaks: store the item so its rare, identifying features survive.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (ICML)
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to a grade-school math problem sharply cuts accuracy for every prompting method. Lexical overlap between the distractor and the problem (shared role names, same topic) raises the harm; the number value in the distractor mattered little.
numbers: GSM-IC (from GSM8K), Codex code-davinci-002 and GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003. Of problems solved by the baseline, no more than 18% were solved for every type of distractor. Fewer than 30% of base problems solved consistently after adding distractors (macro accuracy).
limits: Older models (2022); arithmetic, not memory. Distractor was one sentence.
agent_relevance: Same logic as cue outshining in reverse: cues that look similar to the target pull retrieval off. Filter retrieved notes for relevance before the reader sees them.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Distracted by Irrelevant Context [mitigations]
finding: Three fixes helped. Self-consistency (many samples) nearly always contained the correct answer. Distractors inside the few-shot examples helped. An instruction to ignore irrelevant information helped modestly.
numbers: With 20 samples per problem, at least one of them gave the correct answer in 99.7% of cases (recall of correct answer). The instruction effect was small and mixed in the table (about 1 point either way in several rows).
limits: Instruction deltas read from column-merged text; approximate.
agent_relevance: Sampling several answers and voting is a stronger guard against distractor cues than one instruction.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models? (COLM)
finding: Plain needle-in-haystack is solved almost perfectly, but harder variants with distractor needles (multi-key) and more needles show large drops with length. Retrieval works when the cue is unique and fails when similar rivals are present.
numbers: 17 long-context models, 13 tasks. Only about half of models claiming 32K or more keep satisfactory performance at 32K. GPT-4: claimed 128K, effective 64K. Yi-34B: robust to needle type, degrades with more distractors.
limits: Synthetic tasks; effective length uses a threshold set from a Llama2-7B 4K baseline.
agent_relevance: Uniqueness of the cue matters more than length. Make each memory handle unique within the store.

source: Weller, Boratko, Naim, Lee (2026) On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval (ICLR)
finding: A single-vector embedding of fixed size cannot separate every set of documents a query might ask for. The authors build LIMIT, a trivial 'who likes X' task; state-of-the-art embedders fail while sparse BM25 does well.
numbers: Full LIMIT: models struggle to reach even 20% recall@100. 46-document version: models cannot solve it even at recall@20. Performance rises with embedding dimension. Fine-tuning on in-domain training data lifted recall@10 only from near zero to at most 2.8.
limits: Synthetic attribute task designed to hit the bound.
agent_relevance: A single similarity score cannot hold all the distinctions a memory needs. Add a second route (exact keys, tags, structured filters).

source: Weller et al. (2026) LIMIT [lexical vs synonym test]
finding: Lexical retrieval wins on LIMIT only because words match. Replace each item with a synonym and BM25 collapses, below most neural models. Pure word match is brittle too.
numbers: LIMIT-small synonym version: BM25 drops more than 89%; Qwen3 embedding drops 38.9%.
limits: One synonym mapping made with Gemini 2.5 Pro.
agent_relevance: Neither pure match nor pure similarity is enough. Use both and keep a distinctive handle per item.

source: Thakur et al. (2021) BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models (NeurIPS D&B)
finding: On 18 datasets and 10 systems, BM25 is a robust zero-shot baseline. Re-ranking and late-interaction models do best on average but cost more. Dense and sparse neural models often fall below the best approaches out of domain.
numbers: 18 datasets, 10 retrieval systems, nDCG@10.
quote: BM25 is a robust baseline and re-ranking and late-interaction based models on average achieve the best zero-shot performances
limits: Document retrieval, pre-2022 models. No per-dataset numbers taken.
agent_relevance: Cheap exact-term scoring is a hard baseline to beat. Add a re-ranker if cost allows.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Dense X Retrieval: What Retrieval Granularity Should We Use? (EMNLP)
finding: Indexing atomic, self-contained propositions (one fact each, rewritten to stand alone) beats passage or sentence units for retrieval and for downstream QA. Gains are largest for rare (long-tail) entities. A proposition is a single-fact, de-contextualised key.
numbers: 25% relative Recall@5 gain on EntityQuestions with weak retrievers such as DPR. Downstream QA gains of +2.7 to +2.8 EM@500 for some retriever-reader setups. Gain shrinks as entity frequency rises.
limits: Propositions made by a fine-tuned Flan-T5-large; Wikipedia corpus.
agent_relevance: Write each memory as one atomic claim with its own subject and context named. Fewer rival facts per key means less cue overload.

source: Anthropic (2024) Introducing Contextual Retrieval (engineering blog)
finding: Each chunk gets a 50-100 token LLM-written context (document, period, topic) before embedding and BM25 indexing. This makes each chunk more distinctive and cuts failed retrievals.
numbers: Top-20 failure rate: baseline 5.7%; contextual embeddings 3.7% (35% fewer); plus contextual BM25 2.9% (49% fewer); plus reranking 1.9% (67% fewer). Cost about $1.02 per million document tokens one-time with prompt caching. Datasets: codebases, fiction, ArXiv, science papers.
limits: Vendor blog, not peer reviewed; Gemini Text 004 embeddings; Claude 3 Haiku writes the context; no same-length filler control.
agent_relevance: Direct use of the critique in an agent: add distinguishing context to each stored item at write time, not only match at read time. Compare against same-length filler.

source: Chroma (2025) Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance (technical report)
finding: Across 18 models, lower needle-question similarity makes performance fall faster as input grows; a single distractor already lowers accuracy and four lower it more; distractors are not equally harmful.
numbers: 18 models, 194,480 calls. Needle-question similarity ranges 0.445-0.775 (PG essays) and 0.521-0.829 (arXiv). 8 input lengths x 11 needle positions; no notable position effect. LongMemEval: 306 prompts, about 113k tokens full vs about 300 tokens focused; every model did better on focused prompts.
limits: Company report, per-model scores only in figures; two haystack topics.
agent_relevance: Shorter, focused context beats a long context holding the same fact. Similar-but-wrong notes are the main risk.

source: Chroma (2025) Context Rot [haystack structure]
finding: Shuffled haystacks gave better results than coherent essays in all 18 models. A needle that blends with the topic of its surroundings is harder to find (a distinctiveness effect).
numbers: PG essay haystack: arXiv needles (distinct from haystack) did significantly better than PG needles; in arXiv haystack the difference was minimal. Claude models hallucinated least; GPT models most.
limits: Authors call the shuffle result counterintuitive; only two topics.
agent_relevance: An item that stands out from its neighbours is easier to retrieve. Store contrasting features, not shared ones.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: Streaming related key-value updates and asking only for the last value: accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as the number of competing old values per key grows, even though the right value sits right before the query. This is cue overload in an LLM.
numbers: Updates per key 3 to 400 (log spaced), 46 keys fixed. Larger models decline more slowly. At 400 updates per key the M group dropped to 0% with one exception. Errors move from the update just before the target (low load) to far upstream (medium) to values never shown (high load, hallucination) with primacy bias.
limits: Synthetic key-value streams; the interference subfield covers this more.
agent_relevance: Many items under one key defeat the reader. Keep one distinctive key per fact or overwrite stale values.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length [mitigations]
finding: Prompting did not rescue retrieval. Telling the model to forget earlier updates or to focus forward gave limited gains; the per-key forget prompt shifted errors to values just before the instruction. Asking the model to restate the task first did not change the log-linear trend.
numbers: Prompts tested: per-key forget, soft session reset, forward focus, meta-relevant 'describe the goal' prompt. Trend stayed log-linear across variations.
limits: Exact accuracy deltas are in figures.
agent_relevance: Instructions to ignore are weak; change what is stored or retrieved instead.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs (NeurIPS)
finding: HippoRAG builds a graph of named entities and weights each node by node specificity, 1 over the number of passages it appears in (a local inverse-frequency signal, like IDF). Rare, distinctive entities count more. A computational system built on distinctiveness.
numbers: Single-step retrieval R@2 / R@5 average over MuSiQue, 2Wiki, HotpotQA: HippoRAG (ColBERTv2) 57.4 / 72.9; ColBERTv2 53.9 / 65.6; BM25 46.5 / 58.4; Contriever 46.2 / 59.9. Without node specificity: 54.4 / 67.8. Up to 20% over baselines.
limits: GPT-3.5 for entity extraction; multi-hop QA sets only.
agent_relevance: Weight memory handles by how rare they are. Do not weight a common tag the same as a rare name.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for LLMs (NeurIPS) [node specificity ablation]
finding: Removing node specificity lowers average retrieval by about 3 points at R@2 and 5 points at R@5. The paper text says the gain is on MuSiQue and HotpotQA and almost nil on 2Wiki, but the table rows I read show the biggest drop on 2Wiki.
numbers: Average R@2/R@5 full 57.4/72.9 vs without node specificity 54.4/67.8. Rows read: 2Wiki 70.7/89.1 full vs 62.5/77.5 without; HotpotQA 60.5/77.7 vs 59.9/75.1; MuSiQue 40.9/51.9 vs 40.8/51.9.
limits: Text and table disagree on which dataset benefits; per-dataset claim unresolved. Use the average only.
agent_relevance: Distinctiveness weighting gives a measurable but not large gain.

source: Raaijmakers and Shiffrin (1981) Search of Associative Memory (SAM), Psychological Review 88:93-134
finding: Classic computational model of recall. The chance a cue retrieves an item depends on that cue's strength to the item relative to its strength to all other items (the ratio rule), so a cue linked to many items does worse: cue overload. Encoding match is not the key variable; the competition is.
numbers: No numbers taken this session.
limits: Not opened. Described from memory of the literature; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: The formal ancestor of 'use distinctive keys'. Fan size and rival count should enter the retrieval score.

source: Sparck Jones (1972) A statistical interpretation of term specificity and its application in retrieval (IDF), Journal of Documentation
finding: Origin of inverse document frequency: a term found in few documents discriminates better than a common one. The oldest working machine form of the distinctiveness idea.
numbers: No numbers taken this session.
limits: Not opened. From memory; verify.
agent_relevance: IDF-style weighting is a cheap guard for any memory index.

source: Synthesis of the machine studies read in this file (no new source)
finding: Across the studies read here the pattern agrees: match alone is neither necessary nor sufficient. Literal match helps (NoLiMa), hurts when it points at the wrong item (Shi, Chroma, NoLiMa distractors), and rare or distinctive terms carry more value (Sciavolino, HippoRAG, Dense X).
numbers: Key figures: NoLiMa GPT-4o 99.3 to 69.7; EntityQuestions BM25 72.0 vs DPR 49.7; HippoRAG 72.9 vs 67.8 R@5 without specificity; contextual retrieval 67% fewer failures.
limits: Cross-study comparison; models, tasks and metrics differ.
agent_relevance: Design rule: key each memory with a distinctive handle plus context; keep exact-match and semantic routes; rerank; keep retrieved context short.

source: Gap note: direct LLM tests of outshining or Nairne-style cue distinctiveness
finding: No paper was found that tests the outshining effect or Nairne's cue-distinctiveness account directly on LLMs. Web search quota was exhausted and the arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate limited, so this is an absence in what was reachable, not proof of absence.
numbers: None.
limits: Search coverage limited this session. Nearest LLM work is in the 01 subfolder (Dinh et al. 2026; Chauvet 2024).
agent_relevance: Treat distinctiveness in LLM memory as untested; design a small test: same facts with shared vs unique cue words, with and without a strong cue.
